The Migration Amendment (Regional Processing Arrangements) Bill 2015 provides express statutory authority for the Commonwealth to make payments and take actions to assist regional processing countries—currently Nauru and Papua New Guinea—in processing unauthorized maritime arrivals, with retrospective effect from 18 August 2012.

The opposition leader announced Labor would support the Migration Amendment (Regional Processing Arrangements) Bill, arguing it aligns with Labor’s own policy of offshore processing and regional resettlement to deter dangerous boat voyages and prevent deaths at sea. He criticised the government for rushing the bill, attacked past coalition opposition to Labor’s Malaysia arrangement, and called for an end to dehumanising political rhetoric on asylum seekers.

The speaker argued that the opposition leader's support for the Migration Amendment (Regional Processing Arrangements) Bill 2015 cannot undo seven years of Labor decisions since 2008 that weakened border control and caused tragedy.

The speaker endorsed the Migration Amendment (Regional Processing Arrangements) Bill 2015, arguing that the government's border protection policies—including regional processing, turn-backs, and prioritising refugees from camps over those who can pay people smugglers—have integrity and are supported by former refugees in his electorate of Cowan. He cited 1,000 places for women and children at risk and criticised the opposition's past Malaysia plan as a swap rather than regional processing.

The speaker argued that the Migration Amendment (Regional Processing Arrangements) Bill 2015 is shameful and constitutes a crime against humanity under the Rome Statute, calling for an end to offshore processing, mandatory detention, and temporary visas, and for Australia to grant permanent refuge to asylum seekers found to be fleeing persecution. He also noted he had made a formal complaint to the International Criminal Court regarding the government's actions.

The Migration Amendment (Regional Processing Arrangements) Bill 2015 is necessary to maintain border control; anyone arriving illegally by boat will never be settled in Australia. Previous Labor policies led to 50,000 boat arrivals, over 1,000 deaths at sea, and an $11 billion cost blowout.

The majority agreed with the bill's main idea. In parliamentary jargon, they voted in favour of reading the bill for a [second time](http://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). This means that they can now discuss the bill in more detail. ### What is the bill's main idea? The bill (as amended) makes changes to the assets test for all means tested income support payments, including allowances and pensions. Firstly, it increases the threshold above which your assests are tested (known as "free areas") for the purposes of support payments. In other words, people on allowances or full pensions can have more assets than they currently can before those assets are included in their means testing - but not that much more. See the [bills digest](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1415a/15bd129) for the asset test limits. People on allowances whose assets are above the free areas will no longer be eligible for that allowance while pensioners whose assets are above the free areas will have their pensions reduced at an increased rate. If someone is no longer eligible for a payment as a result of the changes, the bill makes them eligible for a concession card (either a Health Care Card or a Commonwealth Seniors Health Card). Read more in the [bills digest](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1415a/15bd129).

The government's proposed changes to the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Fair and Sustainable Pensions) Bill 2015 will increase asset test thresholds, with single homeowners' threshold rising from $202,000 to $250,000 and couples' from $286,500 to $375,000, meaning 90% of pensioners will be better off or unchanged and 170,000 part-pensioners will move to full pension. The speaker criticised the opposition for lacking solutions and for opposing the bill, which also includes measures on defined benefit income, overseas pension payments, and automatic issuance of Commonwealth seniors health cards to those losing pension eligibility.

The speaker argued that Prime Minister Tony Abbott repeatedly promised no pension cuts before the 2013 election but now supports legislation cutting pensions for 330,000 low-income households and removing 90,000 entirely, calling the government untrustworthy and its deal with the Greens a broken promise.

They proposed instead reducing superannuation tax concessions for high-income earners to save $14.3 billion over a decade, and said Labor would not support most measures but would back $1.5 billion in other savings.

They also defended Labor's past pension increases and criticized the government for targeting pensioners while avoiding revenue measures.

Specific thresholds were cited: for full pension eligibility, the assets-free area rises to $250,000 for single homeowners and $375,000 for couple homeowners, while non-homeowners can have up to $699,000 in assets (couples) or $537,000 (singles) to be better off.

Minister Hunt has claimed repeatedly the biomass that is going to be burnt in forest furnaces is just waste, so we are interested in knowing exactly what is the government's definition of 'waste' or 'residue' in relation to the burning of native forest biomass for electricity. As far as we can see, nothing about this proposal to be burning wood from native forests for energy is about waste. Rather, it is about maintaining, entrenching and expanding industrial scale clear-fell logging that would not otherwise have occurred. It is not about branches, bark and treetops, as we have been misled to believe over the last months. If it were it would be restricted to this and would not include whole logs. In contrast, this legislation is all about allowing the burning of whole logs from native forests for electricity—it is so far from being renewable it is not funny. Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2015 - Third Reading - Pass the bill

The bill adjusts the large-scale renewable energy target to 33,000 gigawatt hours by 2020, aiming for 23.5% of electricity from renewables, increases exemptions for emissions-intensive trade-exposed industries to full exemptions, reinstates native forest wood waste as an eligible renewable source, and removes biennial reviews of the target.

The opposition supported the Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2015 except for part 4, arguing the bill stabilised the renewable energy industry after a "reckless" attack by the Prime Minister, which broke election promises made during negotiations between Minister Wong and then-shadow minister MacFarlane.

The speaker argued in support of the Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2015, which sets a Large-scale Renewable Energy Target of 33,000 gigawatt hours by 2020, resulting in over 23.5% of Australia’s electricity from renewable sources. The bill reduces the target from 41,000 gigawatt hours, reinstates biomass from native forest wood waste as eligible renewable energy, and provides full exemptions from RET costs for emissions-intensive trade-exposed industries like Tomago Aluminium.

The Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2015 reduces the large-scale renewable energy target to 33,000 gigawatt hours by 2020, extends full exemptions for emissions-intensive trade-exposed activities, removes periodic reviews, and reinstates native wood waste as an eligible resource; the speaker supported the bill but opposed including native wood waste, arguing Labor will use the target as a floor to build a more ambitious post-2020 policy.

The Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2015 reduces the renewable energy target from 41,000 to 33,000 gigawatt hours, justified by changed energy use behaviour, industry moving offshore due to higher power prices, and improvements in solar and fossil fuel technology.
The Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2015 reflects a bipartisan agreement between the government and opposition on renewable energy targets.

Labor supported the Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2015, which sets the large-scale renewable energy target at 33,000 gigawatt hours by 2020, projecting $40.4 billion in investment and 15,000 jobs, but opposed the reinstatement of native wood-waste biomass as an eligible renewable source, vowing to move an amendment to exclude it.

The Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2015 rescales the renewable energy target from 41,000 to 33,000 gigawatt hours, provides assistance to emissions-intensive trade exposed industries, and includes wood waste. The speaker supported the first two elements but opposed the inclusion of wood waste.

The speaker argued that renewable energy exists only through subsidies and welfare, and supported the Renewable Energy (Electricity Amendment) Bill 2015, which reduces the large-scale renewable energy target to 33,000 gigawatt-hours by 2020, grants full exemptions for emissions-intensive trade-exposed industries, and reinstates biomass from native forest wood waste as eligible. The speaker also cited the Warburton review's cost estimates and noted the benefit for Sun Metals, a zinc refinery in their electorate.

The bill reduces the renewable energy target from 41,000 to 33,000 gigawatt hours by 2020, increases exemptions for emissions-intensive trade-exposed industries, reinstates native forest wood waste as eligible biomass, and removes biennial reviews. The speaker argued the changes are necessary to prevent penalty payments, industry closures, and to address market distortions from previous Labor government policies that created “phantom credits.”

The speaker argued in support of the Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2015, stating it ends endless reviews and grants full exemptions to emissions-intensive trade-exposed industries. He criticised the coalition for causing an 88% fall in clean energy investment and 21,000 jobs at risk, and claimed Labor's compromise would deliver $10 billion in additional investment and 6,500 jobs.

The speaker opposed the Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2015, arguing it would raise electricity costs for low-income households, waste billions in subsidies, and fail to deliver reliable renewable energy by 2020. He cited a median weekly income of $411 in his electorate, an 87% rise in electricity disconnections to 12,454 households, and cost comparisons of $36 per megawatt hour for coal versus $190 for solar and $120 for wind.

The Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2015 would lock in $20 billion of malinvestment in 2,000 additional wind turbines, despite electricity demand being 20% lower than forecast and the market already oversupplied. The speaker argued that the bill would increase electricity costs, destroy wealth, and that wind turbines are not cost-effective without subsidies, citing a Grattan Institute report finding solar subsidies cost $9 billion more than benefits.

The Labor Party supports the revised Renewable Energy Target of 33,000 gigawatt hours but opposes the inclusion of native wood waste and calls for fixing the self-generation exemption anomaly. The speaker also notes bipartisan efforts involving ministers Hunt and Macfarlane and shadow ministers Bowen and Butler, and highlights that investment in large-scale renewables fell 88% in 2014.

The member for Petrie supported the Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2015, which sets a large-scale renewable energy target of 33,000 gigawatt hours by 2020, increases exemptions for emissions-intensive trade-exposed activities, reinstates native forest wood waste as an eligible renewable energy source, and removes biennial reviews, while noting no changes to household solar and promoting a $20,000 instant tax write-off for small businesses.

The speaker argued that the Abbott government's changes to the Renewable Energy Target protect fossil fuel companies, undermine climate action, and harm jobs, citing 20,000 Australian jobs in renewables and $10 billion in stalled investments. They supported the target as a proven mechanism to reduce carbon emissions, contrasting it with the government's "direct action" policy, which they said cost over $600 per tonne of abatement with little benefit.

The Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2015 was supported as restoring balance to the RET scheme by setting an achievable target, providing investment certainty, and preventing a default that would raise electricity costs. The speaker supported the Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2015 and its amendments, noting a capital strike in renewables over the past 18 months and citing 4,500 jobs in New South Wales’ renewables sector, as well as BlueScope Steelworks’ investment in solar-integrated Colorbond technology. They credited the members for Port Adelaide and Brand for working with the Minister to reach this point.

Opposed the Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2015 for lowering the target, arguing it harms the environment and public interest; supported amendment (4) but opposed burning forest waste for energy, citing Tasmania’s experience where such practices led to widespread deforestation.

The speaker noted Tasmania's 86% renewable energy share and 1,500–2,000 renewable energy jobs, welcomed the RET agreement and exemption for four major industrial users (Bell Bay Aluminium, TEMCO, Nyrstar, Norske Skog), and clarified Labor's opposition to including native forest biomass in the RET while criticising the state Liberal government for sacking forestry workers.

Introduced the Australian Border Force Bill 2015 to create the statutory office of Australian Border Force Commissioner, who will also serve as Comptroller-General of Customs, merging Customs and Immigration into a single front-line agency partly modelled on Operation Sovereign Borders' integrated approach.

Introduced consequential legislation to complete the Australian Border Force integration, citing an Australian Crime Commission estimate that organised crime costs Australia $15 billion annually, extending Law Enforcement Integrity Commissioner oversight to the whole department from 1 July 2015, and allowing resignations to be deferred up to 90 days during misconduct investigations.

Labor supported the Australian Border Force Bill 2015 and related legislation, arguing it fulfills a former Labor government commitment to create a single integrated border entity with no greater powers than existing agencies, and includes integrity measures such as drug testing and serious misconduct provisions.

The speaker argued for abolishing the Australian Customs and Border Protection Service and merging its functions with the Department of Immigration and Border Protection to create the Australian Border Force, citing $480.5 million in funding over four years and a track record of no lives lost at sea and over 200 days without boat arrivals.

The speaker supported the Australian Border Force Bill 2015 and related legislation, arguing they establish the Australian Border Force Commissioner and a single integrated border entity with integrity provisions including drug/alcohol testing, serious misconduct declarations, and mandatory reporting, while acknowledging border workers' dedication.

The speaker endorsed the Australian Border Force Bill 2015, supporting the coalition's national security policies including citizenship revocation for dual nationals involved in terrorism, and argued the bill would create an integrated border force to handle rising cargo and passenger volumes, with projected savings of $180 million over forward estimates and $100 million annually thereafter.

The speaker supported the Australian Border Force Bill 2015, emphasising its importance for Western Australia's border security and highlighting the Cape Class patrol boats built by Austal in Henderson—eight vessels delivered on time and on budget, capable of 28-day patrols and 4,000 nautical mile range.

The speaker supported the Australian Border Force Bill 2015, which merges Customs and Immigration into a single department and establishes an Australian Border Force led by a Commissioner, citing the success of Operation Sovereign Borders in stopping boat arrivals and saving $2.5 billion, and projecting $180 million in efficiencies over the forward estimates.

The speaker supported the Australian Border Force Bill 2015 and its cognate bill, arguing that increased border interactions—44.17% more passenger/crew, 83.59% more air cargo, and 40.6% more sea cargo over the past decade—necessitated the creation of a single integrated Australian Border Force within the Department of Immigration and Border Protection from 1 July. He also criticised the previous government’s border policy, citing 51,798 illegal arrivals and a cost of $11.5 billion, and praised Operation Sovereign Borders.

The speaker argued that the Australian Border Force Bill 2015 and related legislation will improve border security by merging customs and immigration functions under a single commissioner, with projected savings of $180 million over the forward estimates. He contrasted this with the previous Labor government’s border record, citing an $11 billion budget blowout, 50,000 maritime arrivals, over 1,000 drownings at sea, and low cargo examination rates.

The speaker argued for the establishment of the Australian Border Force through the 2015 bills, citing the government's success in stopping illegal boat arrivals (51,000 under Labor, including 8,400 children, with 1,200 lives lost at sea) and getting children out of detention, while also outlining new powers for the Commissioner, drug testing, and misconduct provisions.

The speaker argued that the Customs and Other Legislation Amendment (Australian Border Force) Bill 2015 should be passed to integrate the Department of Immigration and Border Protection with the Australian Customs and Border Protection Service, creating the Australian Border Force by 1 July 2015. The bill is expected to generate $180 million in operating efficiencies and $100 million in annual savings, while strengthening border security against drug smuggling, visa non-compliance, and organised crime.

The speaker argued in favour of the Australian Border Force Bill 2015, which creates a single front-line border enforcement agency combining customs and immigration officers to manage projected increases in travellers and goods. They cited expected efficiencies of $180 million over forward estimates and contrasted the Coalition's border policies with Labor's record of 800 boats and up to 2,000 children in detention.

The speaker supported the Australian Border Force Bill 2015 and related legislation, arguing they would strengthen border protection, save $100 million, and build on Operation Sovereign Borders' success in stopping boat arrivals. They credited the coalition with ending Labor-era detention centre strain in Solomon, citing 800 boats and over 50,000 arrivals, and thanked Ministers Peter Dutton and Scott Morrison.

The speaker argued that the Australian Border Force Bill 2015 establishes a single integrated border agency to enforce customs and immigration laws, criticising Labor’s border policies for leading to 800 boats, 1,200 deaths at sea, and 2,000 children in detention, which the coalition reduced to under 100. He also highlighted the need for integrity provisions to counter organised crime and the creation of a Border Force Counter-Terrorism Unit to intercept passengers of national security concern.

The speaker supported the Australia Border Force Bill 2015 and the Customs and Other Legislation Amendment (Australian Border Force) Bill 2015, arguing the government fulfilled its election commitment to stop boat arrivals. They cited over 240 days without illegal boat arrivals, one boat in the past year compared to 302 in 2013, and projected $180 million in efficiencies from consolidating immigration and customs into the Australian Border Force.

The Australian Border Force Bill 2015 was argued to integrate the Department of Immigration and Border Protection and the Australian Customs and Border Protection Service, generating $180 million in efficiencies over the forward estimates and $100 million per year thereafter, while addressing threats from transnational crime, terrorism, and increased traveller and cargo volumes.

The speaker argued in support of the Australian Border Force Bill 2015, criticising previous Labor government cuts to border protection agencies that reduced air cargo screening from 60% to 10% and enabled the illegal importation of 220 Glock pistols, with 106 still unaccounted for. The bill establishes the statutory office of the Australian Border Force Commissioner to command a new front-line operational border control entity within the Department of Immigration and Border Protection.

The speaker argued that the Australian Border Force Bill 2015 and the Customs and Other Legislation Amendment (Australian Border Force) Bill 2015 establish the Australian Border Force Commissioner, integrate the Department of Immigration and the Australian Customs and Border Protection Service, and strengthen border integrity and law enforcement, with thanks to Mike Pezzullo and Roman Quaedvlieg.
This bill is part of a package that would create a payment scheme for workers with cognitive disabilities whose pay was set by a specific assessment tool at Australian Disability Enterprises.

The package would adjust several Commonwealth laws, including tax and social security rules, so payments are treated as lump sum arrears for tax purposes and are not counted as income for welfare payments.
Eligible workers would need to register by 1 May 2015 and submit applications by 30 November 2015, with payments possible from July 2014.
The bill would amend tax law so payments are eligible for the lump sum in arrears tax offset.
It would change social security law and the Veterans’ Entitlements Act 1986 to exclude payments from income testing, preventing reductions in income support.
It would adjust confidentiality provisions in social security law to allow sharing of personal information for administering the scheme.
Supported employees with intellectual impairment at Australian Disability Enterprises whose wages were set by the Business Services Wage Assessment Tool, and their families and carers.
